sections.h2: Where does Owensboro fit in Kentucky's housing market?
sections.html:
Owensboro is the seat of Daviess County and the fourth most populous city in Kentucky, on U.S. 60 and Interstate 165 about 107 miles southwest of Louisville. The 2020 census counted 60,183 residents, and the Census Bureau estimated 60,892 on July 1, 2025, a rise of only 1.1 percent from the 2020 base. The wider metro area, which also takes in Hancock and McLean counties, was estimated at 116,506.

The 2020-2024 Census figures give a median owner-occupied value of $178,900, a median gross rent of $905 and an owner-occupied rate of 57.4 percent across 25,451 households. Workers spend a mean of 17.1 minutes getting to their jobs.

sections.h2: What is the land and weather like around an Owensboro house?
sections.html:
The city sits in the crook of a bend in the Ohio River, 37 miles southeast of Evansville, Indiana. It covers 20.4 square miles, of which 6.47 percent is water. The settlement began as Yellow Banks, after the color of the bluffs beside the river, was formally established as Owensborough in 1817 and took its shorter modern spelling in 1893.

The climate is humid subtropical, with hot, humid summers and moderately cold winters. Severe weather, including tornadoes, is not unusual through much of the year. An F3 tornado cut through the city on December 9, 1952, so it is worth checking the roof and gutters for storm damage before a house is shown.

  • The city has 26,918 housing units, with 6.7 percent vacant in the 2020 census.
  • Owensboro Public Schools and Daviess County Public Schools both serve the area, along with the Catholic school system.
  • Brescia University, Kentucky Wesleyan College and Owensboro Community and Technical College are based in the city.

sections.h2: Which industries have supported Owensboro homeowners?
sections.html:
Owensboro has a long industrial past. Bourbon distilling, tobacco stemmeries, a wagon works, furniture and light bulb and vacuum tube plants all took turns as major employers, and two distilleries, Glenmore and Green River, are still in operation. A gas pipeline company moved its headquarters here in 1948, and a welding and steel tank firm founded on the riverfront in 1932 is now one of the country's largest suppliers of storage tanks.

sections.h2: What does Owensboro's population say about who buys here?
sections.html:
The median age in Owensboro was 38.1 in the 2020 census, and 18.3 percent of residents were 65 or older. The Census Bureau's newer estimate puts the share aged 65 and over at 19.0 percent. About 34.9 percent of households are made up of one person, and 14.9 percent are one person aged 65 or older, so a good share of sellers are older owners downsizing or heirs settling an estate.

Median selected monthly owner costs are $1,321 for owners with a mortgage and $522 for those without one, and 85.3 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier. The 2020 census counted 25,105 households, of which 29.0 percent had children under 18 at home.

The city carries some civic recognition: it was named an All-America City in 2013, and the Bluegrass Music Hall of Fame and Museum, which won a Governor's Award for Community Arts that year, sits on the riverfront. Evidence of Native American settlement here goes back 12,000 years, and the Ohio River riverfront park carries the name of the first European settler.

sections.h2: How does Owensboro enforce its property maintenance code?
sections.html:
The city enforces a Property Maintenance Code through Public Works. Ordinance 37-2019 amends the original 2011 ordinance and adopts provisions of the 2009 International Property Maintenance Code, and any violation counts as a nuisance. The code covers roughly 24,000 private parcels inside the city limits.

  • Code Enforcement Officers investigate, inspect and document conditions on a property.
  • They can issue a Notice of Violation and then a citation.
  • Owners can appeal, and the city can abate a nuisance and enter property under the ordinance.

If you own a vacant or inherited house in poor shape, resolve any open notice before you sell, or tell the buyer what it covers. Cash buyers often take houses with deferred maintenance, since they plan the repairs themselves.

sections.h2: What does a seller owe at the Daviess County Clerk in Owensboro?
sections.html:
Deeds for Owensboro addresses are recorded at the Daviess County Clerk, and Kentucky's transfer tax under KRS 142.050 is paid by the seller at that time. The rate is fifty cents for each $500 of value, with any fraction counted as a full unit. At the Census median of $178,900 the tax is $179.

Some transfers escape the tax entirely: sales for delinquent taxes, partitions, transfers between spouses in a divorce and foreclosure or deed in lieu of foreclosure. Ask the Daviess County Clerk for the current recording fee, since it changes, and ask the county PVA about your assessment and any exemption you hold before you set a closing date.

sections.h2: When does a cash offer suit an Owensboro house?
sections.html:
Owensboro sellers often have an older house, a river-town location and a limited number of showings, so a direct sale can save months. A cash buyer pays the price in full at closing and does not wait on a lender's appraisal, which matters for houses that need roof, wiring or foundation work.

  • An estate sale where an older owner has died or moved to care and the family lives in another state.
  • A rental house with a departed tenant and a damage list.
  • A house with a Property Maintenance notice that the owner cannot afford to fix.
  • A seller moving for work to Evansville, Louisville or elsewhere on a firm date.

Get the offer in writing and ask the buyer who pays the closing costs. Compare the net with a listing after repairs, carrying costs and the $0.50 per $500 transfer tax, and confirm the payoff on any mortgage with your lender.

sections.h2: Who runs Owensboro, and why does that matter to a seller?
sections.html:
Owensboro is a home rule city and has used a city manager form of government since 1954. Voters elect a mayor to a four-year term and four commissioners to two-year terms, and the commissioners hire a city manager who runs daily operations. Code, permit and utility questions therefore go to city departments, not to the commission directly.

If you want to sell fast, collect the paperwork the buyer will want: the deed, any recorded liens, recent tax bills and notices from Code Enforcement. A clear file moves a sale to closing sooner whether the buyer pays cash or uses a lender.

faqs.q: How many people live in Owensboro?
faqs.a: The 2020 census counted 60,183, and the Census Bureau estimated 60,892 on July 1, 2025. The metro area including Hancock and McLean counties was estimated at 116,506.

faqs.q: How much is the transfer tax on an Owensboro sale?
faqs.a: It is fifty cents per $500 of value, charged to the seller. A sale at Owensboro's $178,900 median value comes to $179 when the partial unit is rounded up.

faqs.q: Who enforces property upkeep in Owensboro?
faqs.a: Code Enforcement Officers in the city's Public Works department. They inspect, issue notices of violation and citations and can abate nuisances under the Property Maintenance Code.

faqs.q: Can I sell an Owensboro house that has a violation notice?
faqs.a: Yes. Read the notice, note the deadline to fix or appeal, and disclose it to the buyer. A cash buyer may agree to take the repair on after closing.
At the Daviess County Clerk, since the county records land for all of its cities. Ask that office for its current recording fee before closing.
